question: Xi Jinping out before 2027?
description:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if China's General Secretary of the Communist Party, Xi Jinping, is removed from power for any length of time between July 3, 2025, and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping will be considered removed from power if he announces his resignation from his role as General Secretary, or is otherwise dismissed, detained, disqualified, or otherwise loses his position or is prevented from fulfilling his duties as General Secretary within this market's timeframe.

The primary resolution source for this market will be a consensus of credible reporting.

eventMetadata.context_description: Xi Jinping’s entrenched dominance within the Chinese Communist Party underpins the strong trader consensus against his removal before 2027. Ongoing anti-corruption purges across the military, Politburo, and Central Committee have removed potential rivals without eroding his authority, while recent plenums and the Beidaihe conclave have focused on preparations for the 21st Party Congress rather than any transition. At age 73, Xi faces no formal term limits following the 2018 constitutional change and shows no public signals of stepping aside, with elite networks aligned through loyalty criteria and generational norms applying mainly to subordinates. The opaque system leaves room for low-probability shocks such as a sudden health crisis or severe economic dislocation that could trigger elite realignment, though recent developments indicate continuity through a likely fourth term at the 2027 congress.

eventMetadata.context_description: Trader consensus prices a fragmented 2028 Democratic field tightly, with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 22.1 percent, Gavin Newsom and Jon Ossoff near 15 percent, and Kamala Harris at 7.4 percent. A crowded bench of governors, senators, and House members, none yet declared, keeps probabilities compressed as early positioning intensifies ahead of the DNC-approved calendar that elevates South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan, and Virginia. Mixed signals between national polls favoring Harris and prediction markets rewarding perceived fundraising strength or progressive enthusiasm sustain the closeness. Recent primary wins, coy statements on runs, and calendar adjustments have produced incremental shifts without creating separation, leaving room for future polling trends, candidate announcements, or midterm results to reorder the field.
